text:
ana: Heads-up — planning a staged cutover for the new routing layer tomorrow 0900 UTC. Want to lock down telemetry gates + SLA escape hatch before we flip any traffic.

tim: +1. can we define the exact health signals that will block progression? latency, error-rate, and tail-p99 cpu?

ana: thinking: 1) p95 latency > baseline + 40% for 5m, 2) error-rate > 0.5% for 1m or 3x baseline, 3) sustained queue growth on ingress workers for 2min. those three should auto-hold.

josh: curious about user-affinity implications — staging will shard by tenant. if we hold, do we roll back just those tenants or global?

ana: plan is staged by tenant cohort. rollback/escape hatch should be per-cohort. global only if control plane is unhealthy.

mike: ops concern: if cohort rollback is per-tenant we need a fast surgeon action. who owns the manual swap? runbook needs exact commands and an automated safety API.

josh: agree. we should expose a single `POST /safety/v1/escrow` with body {cohort, reason, action: rollback|pause|reroute}. that way on-call can trigger safely.

ana: +1 on safety API. add auth via mTLS and audit log. also link to runbook snippet in alert payload.

mike: on-call notes: add an alert variant that fires before auto-hold with TTL 60s — basically a 1-minute heads up ping to the sRE channel so humans can intervene before automated action.

ana: good call. we should have a staged escalation: warn -> auto-hold -> auto-rollback. during warn window, include suggested mitigations and a `Cancel AutoHold` quick action.

josh: telemetry side: we'll need a rolling-window evaluator to avoid noisy single-point flips. suggest 2m lookback with 30s step, require 3 consecutive steps to trigger. reduces flapping.

mike: also ensure canary has split limits: max cohort qps, min healthy replica count, and backpressure threshold. don't let canary eat capacity.

ana: ops decision: default cohort size 1% traffic for 10m, then 5% for 10m, then 25% for 20m with manual approval for >25%. this keeps risk bounded.

josh: interface boundary question: who owns the rollout state? controller or router? existing infra stores assignment in control plane; controller should own rollout state and publish desired weights to router. routers just consume weights and enforce local constraints.

mike: +1. router should also expose local safety feedback (eg: kernel queue depth, gpu util) back to controller so decisions can be holistic.

ana: ops/runbook excerpt: 
```
# quick rollback
curl -X POST https://control-plane.internal/safety/v1/escrow \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -d '{"cohort":"cohort-3","action":"rollback","reason":"p95 spike"}'
```

mike: add a remediation checklist in the runbook: check model variant, probe at /health, confirm KV cache saturation, rotate to smaller batch config.

josh: testing: we should run chaos-tests that simulate partial probe failures and network partitions. ensure auto-hold doesn't cascade into mass rollbacks.

ana: agreed. also add a 'graceful degrade' path: if model variant fails but baseline still healthy, route cohort to baseline with a soft throttle and mark for post-mortem.

sre-bot: deploy-bot: canary controller v0.7 scheduled for 2024-06-25T09:00Z. Automated safety will be enabled in notify-only mode for the first hour.

mike: notify-only first hour is good — we can validate alerting and the cancel quick-action flow.

josh: follow-up action items: 1) ana write safety API spec, 2) tim define exact alert rules, 3) mike update runbook with curl snippet + checklist, 4) josh add chaos tests and rolling-window evaluator.

ana: will do. I'll post PR with spec and runbook link by EOD. :thumbsup:
